title: Stress and Performance in Medical Students During Advanced Life Support Simulation-Based Training: A Comparison of Low- and High-Appearance-Fidelity Manakins
summary:
Simulation training is used in medical education to allow students to practise the management of emergency situations in a realistic setting. Such training can cause stress in students. It is currently unclear how the realistic appearance of the training manikin affects students' stress responses and performance.

This study investigates whether a highly realistic-looking training manikin, compared with a conventional training manikin, affects stress responses in medical students. Participants are randomly assigned to one of the two groups and complete two standardized emergency and resuscitation exercises in small teams. Physical stress responses, perceived stress, performance during the exercises, and team communication are assessed.
conditions: Stress response during simulation-based resuscitation training in healthy medical students

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Medical students at Brandenburg Medical School who have completed the “Emergency Medicine 2” module in the 5th semester.
Exclusion criteria:
Pregnancy or breastfeeding; acute or chronic psychiatric or neurological disorders; use of medications that may affect the investigated stress parameters (e.g., glucocorticoids or psychotropic medications).
